articles.title: Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England | John Harris
articles.summary: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers. We can make this the new normal – and we should. A fortnight or so ago, my two teenage kids and I set out on a three-night visit to the Peak District where temperatures were hovering at a comparatively tepid 28C.
body: The next bit might sound self-parodically Guardian-esque, but what the hell: in its own way, the most striking sight was the diversity of the scores of people rambling up, down and along. Women in their 20s wearing hijabs picnicked on giant rocks, while multiracial gaggles of young men attempted to race to the top; solo and shirtless white fitness freaks and retirement-age dog walkers took their places alongside them. With plenty of justification, country walking has long been typified as one of the most monoculturally white pursuits there is. But here – presumably because of the relatively close proximity of Manchester and Sheffield – things looked different.
points: The landscape was striking, but so was the diversity of the hikers.
We can make this the new normal – and we should.

articles.title: Readers reply: Is it inevitable that consumerism will literally fill up the planet?
articles.summary: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions considers whether there is sufficient global physical capacity for all our discarded and worn-out purchases. • This week’s question: If all car tyres were filled with CO2, would this cut atmospheric carbon significantly?
body: Jared Diamond’s Collapse examines previous civilisations that collapsed, why, and the archaeological evidence that sheds light on the consequences. In all cases the cause was one or more of the following: climate change, interruption of trade routes, war or disease. In all of the cases, there was evidence of cannibalism. James Lovelock (of Gaia fame) opined that our current trajectory would result in our species being reduced “to a few breeding pairs in the Arctic where the climate remains tolerable”.

Our global society will inevitably end. There will be far fewer of us, and our lives will be far harder, than now. We will consume less because there will be less to consume. But the world won’t end. When most of us are gone, the planet and its ecosphere will recover. It will take hundreds of years, but the future of the planet is assured. Ours, not so much.
No, the Earth won’t ever get over-full of manufactured items, and storage space is not really the problem. It’s much more serious.
Unsustainable consumption, in all its many forms, is the issue here, under every political and economic system. Consumer capitalism is very much part of the problem, but it runs much deeper.

articles.title: Aardman’​s Peter Lord and David Sproxton: ‘At the Oscars, I went to the gents and had a pee with Jack Nicholson!’
articles.summary: The ​s​tudio’s co-founders on ​accidentally creating Morph, not wanting a yacht in the Maldives and being each other’s best ally. Peter Lord and David Sproxton are the founders of Aardman Animations.
body: We’re sitting there smiling happily and in front of us are some puppets, because that’s what we’re famous for. In this case, Fowler and Babs from Chicken Run, and Morph.

In 2006, we were in between productions – we had finished Chicken Run and the next was Flushed Away and Wallace & Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit. I was going to California quite a lot to jolly the production along. While it was exciting to be in Hollywood, we never aspired to be part of it when we started Aardman.

I was born in Bristol, but when I was nine my parents moved to Sydney, Australia. As a small, not very sporty boy, I found the school system there fairly terrifying. Then, when I was 12, we ended up in suburban Surrey. My new school was a very old-fashioned place where teachers wore gowns. On my first day, there was only one spare seat in the class. It was next to Sproxton, brackets, DA. By chance, we also got off at the same train stop, which was Walton-on-Thames.

articles.title: The 7 Best Airbnbs in Morocco Include Stately Riads
articles.summary: An Airbnb in Morocco gives you lots of space, privacy, and (if you book one of our favorite riads) unique architectural charm. Here, seven favorites.
body: Wandering around Morocco’s medinas involves a bit of sensory overload. The small, winding alleyways are full of life: local artisans parade their crafts; spice merchants stand behind conical mounds of brightly colored saffron, paprika, and turmeric; women sell fresh herbs and Argan oil; young children on bikes weave through it all with almost unbelievable ease.

Once you look beyond it all, you begin to notice the streets themselves; specifically the heavy wooden doors, sometimes intricately carved, other times plain and unassuming. It’s behind these doors that the noise of the streets and souks stops. A few open into cafés or museums, but many of them lead into private homes—multi-floor spaces where windows and balconies overlook central courtyards filled with citrus trees, decorative tiling, and sparkling pools and fountains. Welcome to the Moroccan riad.

articles.title: Rihanna Runs It Back in a 2000s-era Rihanna Staple
articles.summary: While everyone else engages in the great summer shorts debate, Rihanna opts to keep it classic on a night out in New York.
body: What side of the summer shorts spectrum have you landed on? Are you Team Itty Bitty with Charli? Big Shorts Brigade? A jorts disciple like J-Law and Margot Robbie? While everyone engages in the great shorts debate, Rihanna keeps it classic in a denim mini-skirt.

The pop star and beauty mogul—who was spotted leaving the Four Seasons Hotel in New York City with partner A$AP Rocky and their children on Friday—opted for a dark-wash denim skirt with the inside pockets and raw hems on show from Danish designer (and Marni CD) Meryll Rogge. She paired the nostalgic staple with a candy pink Miu Miu track jacket with the collar popped (also, very aughts) and her fave pair of Amina Muaddi snakeskin strappy sandals. (Because whether day or night, red carpet or jaunt to Giorgio Baldi, you can trust Rih is wearing some kind of animal print.) Accessories were signature: a gold choker, gold and diamond earrings, and rose-tinted aviator sunglasses.
Glam was also textbook Rihanna, wearing her hair in voluminous curls, with a blood-red manicure and white pedicure, plus a glossed brown lip.

articles.title: A First Look At Sézane’s “New Era” Autumn Collection
articles.summary: Vogue hears from Sézane founder Morgane Sezalory about the brand’s new era. Expect trenches, denim and suede accessories aplenty.
body: It’s well known that Sézane’s founder, Morgane Sézalory, never set out to create a “brand”–in the traditional sense, anyway. The business grew organically: Sézalory’s first project was Les Composantes, a curated eBay store specializing in vintage, which eventually evolved into designing clothing inspired by her favorite pre-loved pieces. From there, Sézane’s now-recognizable visual identity was born.

“I just wanted to find a way to work and create a job that made sense for me,” she tells Vogue. “I think if I’d had more awareness and more maturity, I would have thought that it was impossible. It was very instinctive and organic, without a strategy.”

Whether intended or not, Sézalory has now built a profitable global brand, which she has recently pivoted in a “new direction”, having watched it evolve over 13 years. For several (mainly personal) reasons– the details of which she outlined in an article for Vogue Business —Sézalory spent a period of reflection to decide how she wanted Sézane to continue.
points: Vogue hears from Sézane founder Morgane Sezalory about the brand’s new era.

articles.title: 17 Dreamy Miami Airbnbs in South Beach, Wynwood, and Beyond
articles.summary: These standout properties feature sprawling pools, sleek amenities, and walkable addresses.
body: I’ve always liked Miami best with a little room to spread out. I grew up coming here on family vacations, then came back for solo escapes, girls’ trips, and romantic weekends by the beach. Somehow, I still find myself falling for the city’s distinct combination of pastel Art Deco buildings, swaying palm trees, warm ocean air, and vibrant neighborhoods that feel like their own little universes.

Hotels can of course be fabulous here, but there’s something especially fun about having your own Miami address for a few days. A Miami Airbnb gives you the space to make coffee in your pajamas, open the doors to a pool or garden, pile everyone onto a sofa after the beach, and actually unpack instead of living out of a suitcase. I’m talking a leafy Coconut Grove hideaway, a glossy Brickell apartment with skyline views, or a colorful family house with a pool that has the potential to make leaving for dinner feel like a chore.
These are the Airbnbs I'd genuinely want to stay at in Miami—from breezy beach bases to character-filled homes that make a weekend away feel like a proper escape.

articles.title: How Our Editors Pick the Best New Restaurants
articles.summary: Editor in chief Jamila Robinson reflects on how the Best New Restaurants of 2026 gave us new ways to eat, gather, and see the world.
body: The question I’m asked most often is, “How does a restaurant get on ‘the list?’” The list can be any compilation of notable restaurants, including awards, star ratings, rankings, or media honors, such as Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants (the 2026 installment of our list publishes Monday, August 24th—check back in tomorrow).

My answers change every year, depending on the kinds of restaurants that open, the trend lines that emerge, and even the whispered wisdom at dinner parties or the buzz on social media. Earning a spot on the list can come down to thoughtful and seamless hospitality, such as a shawl offered in a cold dining room, or the box of chic reading glasses brought to me by a server who noticed I was doing a backbend trying to decipher a weeny menu typeface at a recent dinner in Stockholm.

articles.title: From Sophia Loren to Monica Bellucci, 19 Times Italian Bombshells Ruled the Venice Film Festival
articles.summary: From Sophia Loren to Monica Bellucci, we look back at the Venice Film Festival’s most stylish attendees from decades past.
body: Just as Cannes has its effortlessly chic French girls, Venice Film Festival has always been the undisputed domain of the Italian bombshell. Since the showcase’s inception nine decades ago, these impossibly glamorous women have shimmied off their private water taxis and onto the Lido in showstopping ball gowns, with dramatic cat eyes and lashings of mascara, their hair teased up to perfection and eye-wateringly expensive jewels draped around their necks. Among them were Fellini heroines like Claudia Cardinale; Michelangelo Antonioni’s bewitching muse Monica Vitti; the always elegant Sophia Loren; and Monica Bellucci, still the very definition of va-va-voom style.
As we count down to the event’s 83rd edition, we look back at their most dazzling moments from festivals past.
